title: OpenAI Memory vs. LangMem vs. Letta (MemGPT) vs. Mem0: Which Performs Best?
summary: AI memory benchmark comparing Mem0, OpenAI Memory, LangMem, and Letta (formerly MemGPT) for LLM long-term memory, with reconciled, current LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and BEAM scores.
body_markdown:
Long-term memory is no longer just about storing conversation history. The strongest memory systems combine selective extraction, hybrid retrieval, entity linking, and token efficiency.


Mem0’s[latest memory algorithm](https://mem0.ai/research) uses single-pass ADD-only extraction, multi-signal retrieval, and built-in entity linking. Across current benchmarks, it reports strong accuracy while keeping retrieved context under 7,000 tokens per query.

## **Why This Matters?**


LLMs can stream text fluently, but they still lose continuity once useful context falls outside the active window. Real agents need to remember preferences, timelines, decisions, and facts across days or weeks.


The production question is no longer “can we store memory?” It is “can we retrieve the right memory, at the right time, without stuffing the prompt?”


That is why memory systems are now evaluated across three practical constraints:


-


Accuracy on long-term recall


-


Latency during retrieval and response generation


-


Token cost per query


A memory layer that is accurate but expensive is hard to scale. A fast but shallow memory layer will miss the details that make agents feel useful.


## **Methodology & Why Numbers Differ Across Sources**


The numbers in this post come from a specific benchmark run, not a general claim about "Mem0's accuracy" that holds across every version and setup. Before comparing scores, it's worth being precise about what was actually tested.


These numbers come from Mem0's[open-source memory-benchmarks suite](https://mem0.ai/research) which runs each benchmark through the same three steps every time: it ingests conversations into Mem0, letting the system extract facts, embed them, and link entities; it searches that stored memory for each test question using a blend of semantic similarity, BM25, and entity boost; then it generates an answer from what got retrieved and has a separate judge model score that answer against ground truth. The scores in this post come from running that pipeline against the managed Mem0 Platform on its v3 memory pipeline, at a retrieval depth of Top 200.


That last detail, the retrieval depth, is also the simplest explanation for why you'll see other Mem0 numbers floating around that don't match these. The suite's own documentation is upfront that its scores aren't absolute: they move with embedding model quality, with how capable the extraction and judge models are, and with how deep you set that top-k cutoff. Run LongMemEval on the self-hosted pipeline and swap only the extraction model, keeping the same embedder and judge, and the overall score moves from 91.0% with GPT-5 down to 88.6% with Gemma 4 31B. So if a third-party comparison shows Mem0 scoring lower, the more likely explanation is a shallower top-k, a lighter extraction model, or a smaller embedder, not an error in either post.


The suite's` results/platform/` and` results/oss/` directories also carry the full per-question evaluation data behind every score in this post, if you want to see the work directly.

## **Benchmark Setup**


The current Mem0 benchmark suite evaluates memory across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and BEAM.


-


[LoCoMo](https://mem0.ai/research#:~:text=BENCHMARKS-,LoCoMo,-1%2C540%20questions%20%E2%80%A2%205) **** tests memory recall across multi-session conversations, including single-hop, multi-hop, open-domain, and temporal questions.


-


[LongMemEval](https://mem0.ai/research#:~:text=LOCOMO-,LongMemEval,-500%20questions%20%E2%80%A2%206) **** evaluates single-session recall, assistant recall, preference recall, knowledge updates, temporal reasoning, and multi-session memory.


-


[BEAM](https://mem0.ai/research#:~:text=LONGMEMEVAL-,BEAM,-BEAM%201M%3A%20700) **** tests memory at 1M and 10M token scales. It is especially relevant for production because it cannot be solved by simply expanding the context window.


The key metrics are:


-


benchmark accuracy


-


average tokens per query

## **What Changed in the Memory Architecture**


Mem0’s current algorithm has three major pieces.


-


**Single-pass ADD-only extraction:** The system extracts new memories in one pass and only adds facts. It does not overwrite or delete older memories during extraction. When information changes, the new fact is stored alongside the old one, preserving history. This approach to preserving rather than silently overwriting older facts is also what keeps memory from[going stale](https://mem0.ai/blog/stale-ai-agent-memory-and-how-mem0-dream-fixes-it) as an agent runs for months.


-


**Multi-signal retrieval:** Search combines semantic similarity, BM25 keyword matching, and entity matching. The signals are fused into one final score.


-


**Built-in entity linking:** External graph memory has been replaced by entity linking inside the memory stack. Entities are extracted from memories, stored in a parallel entity collection, and used to boost relevant results during search. This entity layer is also what makes it possible to[resolve the same person or account across sessions](https://mem0.ai/blog/cross-session-identity-resolution-in-agent-memory) .
Together, ADD-only extraction, multi-signal retrieval, and entity linking cover semantic and episodic memory well. They don't yet cover[procedural memory](https://mem0.ai/blog/procedural-memory-explained-teaching-ai-agents-how-to-perform-tasks) i.e. the reusable, step-by-step routines an agent learns and reuses.

## **Summary**


Large context windows delay forgetting, but they do not solve memory problems. A production memory layer has to decide what to store, how to preserve changes over time, and how to retrieve the right facts cheaply.


Mem0


Production memory layer with ADD-only extraction and hybrid retrieval


Best balance of accuracy, latency, and token efficiency


OpenAI Memory


Built-in memory inside ChatGPT


Fastest setup, limited developer control


LangMem


Open-source memory toolkit


Useful for experimentation and custom memory workflows


Letta


Memory paging architecture


Strong conceptual model for context management


The strongest pattern is selective memory plus hybrid retrieval. Mem0’s latest architecture reflects that direction: ADD-only extraction, entity linking, and multi-signal search under a practical token budget.


If your agent needs to live longer than its context window, memory is no longer optional infrastructure. It is part of the core agent stack.


## **Frequently Asked Questions**


**Q. Why do third-party benchmarks show different Mem0 scores?**


Usually because of SDK version, harness, or replication differences rather than a real contradiction. See the Methodology section above for the specific reasons scores can diverge across sources, and the Reproducing Current Mem0 Behavior section if you want to verify these numbers yourself.


**Q. Does Mem0 still support graph memory?**


Standalone graph memory configuration (` enable_graph` ,` graph_store` ) has been removed from the current Mem0 OSS SDK. The relationship-aware recall it used to provide is now handled by built-in entity linking, described under "What Changed in the Memory Architecture" above.


**Q. How does Mem0 compare to other memory tools like Zep or Letta?**


Mem0 differs from Zep and Letta in retrieval strategy and architecture, covered in more depth in dedicated comparisons: see[Mem0 vs Zep](https://mem0.ai/compare/mem0-vs-zep) and[Mem0 vs Letta](https://mem0.ai/compare/mem0-vs-letta) for the full breakdown.
